body:
We were fortunate enough that the full, extended version of the masterpiece Kill Bill has finally arrived in theaters in our country. This edition combines the two previously released volumes into one long film, with a handful of small additions and minor changes. The Kill Bill films are widely regarded as a monumental achievement in modern cinema, and this newly screened combined version - arriving on the big screen for the first time some 20 years later - manages to surpass even the original form. Yes, it is a long film, but when you sit in the theater seat, realize you still have three and a half hours left of this creation, and find yourself not wanting a single minute of it to end, you understand there's something truly special happening here.

An interesting detail is that this story was never originally intended to be two separate films. Quentin Tarantino wrote, shot, and envisioned it as one long (very long) revenge epic, made up of two distinct halves - a first half that is more action-driven and energetic, and a second half that is slower, more dramatic, and dialogue-heavy (classic Tarantino style). Only in the editing stage, when it became clear that the full version crossed the four-hour mark, did the studio and production team decide to split it into two "volumes" in order to avoid significant cuts.

To Tarantino's credit, even as two separate films - as most of us have known them until now - the story works brilliantly, particularly thanks to the different tone of each half. Still, Tarantino has always considered Kill Bill a single film within his filmography, and now we finally get to witness his original vision: a massive, one-of-a-kind cinematic epic.

Does it work? Yes. Absolutely.

This is probably the longest film I've ever watched. And I don't say that lightly - this is one of the finest cinematic creations I've ever had the privilege of experiencing. As someone who has loved the original films since a young age, I was thrilled to finally see them on the big screen for the first time; but beyond that, experiencing the story as one unified piece, as Tarantino intended, is an entirely different experience. This fusion of both films into a single work truly offers everything: sharp Tarantino-style dialogue, breathtaking stylized action, plenty of over-the-top violence, and many intimate moments where the story breathes naturally and explores its characters in depth - making every payoff along the way feel fully earned.

Visually - the film is flawless. From a screenplay perspective - flawless as well. Musically - flawless. The soundtrack blends its iconic songs with several beautiful cues borrowed from older works by Ennio Morricone, and even a touch of original music by the RZA. And of course, we cannot ignore the cast packed with talented actors, led by Uma Thurman, who carries the film proudly in one of the most iconic performances in modern cinema.

Much has been said about how this film borrows (some even use the word "steals") various ideas - especially visual ones - from older movies. The funny thing is that Tarantino has never tried to hide the fact that his films, and Kill Bill in particular, are deeply influenced by other artists' work. On the contrary - over the years he has openly said that he "steals from every movie ever made," often citing the idea that "great artists steal." For him, this isn't an admission of intellectual theft but an artistic method in itself: taking elements from different genres he loves and blending them into a conscious homage to the cinema he grew up on - a cinematic love letter rather than a lack of originality - and personally, I appreciate that approach quite a lot.

Above all, the film was born from Tarantino's immense love for 1960s and 1970s genre cinema, and serves as a collage of influences he absorbed over years of devoted viewing - the films that shaped him into the filmmaker he is today. It combines clear inspirations from samurai films and classic kung-fu cinema, entire sequences of Japanese animation, Hollywood spectacle, Italian western music, exaggerated (yet gorgeous) combat choreography, and even an episodic narrative structure that is rarely seen in modern cinema anymore. In this way, the film is less concerned with being "original" in the literal sense, and more of a self-aware carnival of cinematic traditions drawn from diverse styles - one that manages both to honor them and revive them for audiences who might never have encountered them otherwise - while ultimately creating a unique mosaic stamped with Tarantino's unmistakable touch.

Whether you've already watched the original films a hundred times since they came out, or you've never seen them at all - don't miss this remarkable cinematic event. Yes, it's a very long film, but it's probably one of the best things you'll ever watch. Tarantino crafted an incredible story and brought it to life in a way only he can, and in this combined, complete version his full vision finally comes through in its optimal form, delivering an unforgettable viewing experience.

Finally, we have the director's true vision-exactly as Quentin Tarantino originally intended: as one single, cohesive film. I am both jealous and curious about how this was experienced by people who had never seen Kill Bill Vol. 1 and Vol. 2 before. My only real complaint is the fact that I had already seen both parts, so the element of pure surprise was missing. That is precisely why I deliberately avoided looking up the differences between the versions beforehand, just to save at least a small part of that excitement for the theater. I simply had to experience this on the big screen.

While watching, I had a strong feeling that this version was significantly more violent and bloodier-if that is even possible with Tarantino-and I was not wrong. With the added scenes, more explicit fights, and gallons of blood, the film now functions as one epic journey. It is a tale of revenge that expands in both depth and breadth, giving us everything in one place: a masterfully developed plot, unforgettable characters, and, of course, brilliantly directed violence. Even though it is an exceptionally long piece of cinema, there is no way it gets boring for a single second.

The entire project is drenched in Tarantino's unmistakable signature: the non-linear plot divided into chapters, high drama, fantastic dialogue, and his famous, seemingly "pointless" conversations that build the atmosphere so perfectly. The author once again pays homage to cinema, skillfully blending tributes to classic kung fu movies and spaghetti westerns. The fact that a large portion of the film is not even in English only proves the massive scale of this project and the immense effort put into it. However, I must admit that this is not a film for everyone. The runtime of over four hours and the gargantuan amount of violence will push some general audiences away, but for true cinephiles and fans of Tarantino's style, this is an unmissable theatrical experience.

Just let yourself be entertained. Imagination, creativity, homage, recycling, all together to give us an immense enjoyment. With or without references, it is an appreciable work. I've watched Kill Bill Vol 1 7 times (8 if you count this), if you asked me before watching this if Kill Bill Vol 1 can get any better I'd say no, no way, it's already a masterpiece. But after seeing this I stand corrected. While there's no big change to anything in particular, the few small changes are just enough to make it even better than it already was. The first change you'll notice is an extra 10 minute animated sequence that shows O-Ren Ishii getting revenge on the man that killed her parents. It's animated beautifully and gives O-Ren's character even more depth than she already had. Secondly you'll notice that the legendary fight scene at the House of Blue Leaves is now in full color. With this scene in full color you get to really see the carnage that The Bride creates. You see guys heads being chopped off and geysers of red blood bursting from their neck. You see limbs chopped off with bursts of red blood. You fully see the red blood soaked floor of the building and the red bloody water of the pond. It makes the scene so much more impactful. The third change you see, albeit a minor one, is you actually see how The Bride interrogates Sofia for information. Which of course includes her asking her questions and in turn chopping her arm off for not answering. But the last change and by far most important is at the end of Volume 1, Bill makes no mention of The Brides child still being alive. That small change not only improves Volume 1 but drastically improves Volume 2. Originally you go into Volume 2 technically ahead of The Bride as you know about her kid and she doesn't. But that small change puts us on equal footing with The Bride. It makes the scene of her coming through the door to her child not just shocking and impactful to her but to us, the audience. Before seeing this I'd argue that Volume 1 & 2 are clearly two films and shouldn't count as one. Now, after seeing this, in no way can I say that, they so clearly go together as one film. This is no doubt the definitive way to watch and experience Kill Bill. It's an absolute masterpiece in my opinion.
